lines.narration: The last section is an essay on a speech - nothing in it reduces to four letters.
Her own fingers go between her lips. She is not sick; she is making herself sick.
She buckles until the whole row is watching, and asks to be let home.
Leave now and her score is cancelled, the proctor tells her. She goes anyway, walked out in tears.
Bag on her shoulder she hurries down the corridor. A suited man rushes past: somebody has started looking.
She climbs the stairs while a suited man crosses the lobby, phone at his ear, telling someone he cannot see her.
In the station she sends a coded line about a speech transcript. In Bangkok the alert lands on a phone on cardboard.
She drops to her knees on the station floor and hammers out another block.
Grace types the phrase into search and Nelson Mandela speech transcripts fill the screen. The code opens.
Answer slips go into the rank of motorbike taxis, and the riders pull away.
Her screen reads C A B B. She stops dead on the empty platform.
Commuters hurry past her legs. Bank is gone, so she keeps sending alone, a tear running down her face.
A scuffle, and her backpack is on the floor with the suited man over it. She swallows and faces him.
A staff member tells her what is coming. Another Thai candidate has already admitted carrying a phone in. Her score is gone, and at worst she sits the exam again.
Through the glass she watches Bank answer them. Whatever he gives them, her name is not in it. She turns away.
At Bangkok arrivals Pat has a party waiting: Bank is arrested, their score is banked, and she only has to sit the exam again. She has changed her mind.
Grace puts out a hand to shake on it. Lynn walks straight past both of them.
Her father walks up at the terminal doors and asks where her boyfriend is - he wants the boy over for dinner.
He pulls her into a hug and she breaks, sobbing on his shoulder - everything she has carried since Sydney, out at once.
The party she is not at: balloons, confetti, and matching shirts printed with the score they bought. STIC 1460.
A message from Pat: Bank has already drawn his million and her share is waiting. Lynn left the chat.
A scholarship banner with Bank's face goes up on a school wall; inside, he is head-down at a desk.
The laundry has been rebuilt - new machines still in bubble wrap, a new sign over the door. Mister Bank.
A door opens onto the back workshop. Bank waits against a bench and tells her to come in. She stays put.
He called her for a reason: has she applied for GAT/PAT, because he has a job he wants her on.
He holds out a yellow leaflet: the national exam, every school in the country on the same day. She asks how much he needs.
It is not about enough, he says, but about what he can do from here. A million this time, and getting caught would not mean jail.
She says no. He turns square to her: refuse, and he will see her cut off from the exam that sends her abroad.
And not just her - Grace, Pat and every client who sat it. Her hand is on the door handle. She stops.
One more thing, he says. Her father would be very sad. Her eyes shut, then open flat.
In a white corridor her father sits beside her, head bowed. She turns away, close to tears.
He lifts his head and gives her a small smile, two chairs at the end of an empty corridor.
They walk her past the suits to a camcorder on a tripod.
She sits down across the white table and tells them everything. Bank's threat still stands; she chooses this anyway - and it costs her the exam, the money and him.
